content: 1. In regions where tuberculosis (TB) is endemic, such as developing countries, and in cases with a high clinical suspicion of tuberculous pericarditis, initiating empirical anti-tuberculosis therapy is considered appropriate even before a definitive diagnosis is established. 2. In developed countries where TB is not endemic, empirical anti-tuberculosis therapy should generally not be initiated without a confirmed diagnosis. 3. The World Health Organization (WHO) no longer recommends omitting ethambutol during the intensive phase of treatment for patients with non-cavitary, smear-negative pulmonary TB (PTB) or extrapulmonary TB (EPTB) who are known to be HIV-negative. 4. For new TB patients with suspected or confirmed high levels of isoniazid resistance, specific treatment regimens should be followed. 5. Systematic reviews have shown that daily dosing during the intensive phase of TB treatment, followed by twice-weekly dosing during the continuation phase, is equally effective. However, twice-weekly dosing is not operationally recommended. 6. Daily intensive-phase dosing may help prevent acquired drug resistance in TB patients starting treatment with isoniazid resistance. 7. Patients with isoniazid resistance treated with thrice-weekly intensive-phase dosing have significantly higher risks of treatment failure and acquired drug resistance compared to those treated with daily dosing. 8. Previously treated TB patients should receive an 8-month regimen with first-line drugs. 9. Monitoring the response to multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) treatment should involve both sputum smear microscopy and culture, rather than microscopy alone. 10. Rapid drug susceptibility testing (DST) for isoniazid and rifampicin, or rifampicin alone, is recommended over conventional testing or no testing at the time of TB diagnosis, depending on available resources. 11. Ideally, DST should be performed for all patients at the start of treatment to determine the most appropriate therapy. However, universal access to DST has not yet been achieved globally. 12. Sputum specimens for DST should be obtained from all previously treated patients and all individuals living with HIV diagnosed with active TB, especially in areas with moderate or high MDR prevalence. 13. Rapid molecular-based DST can confirm or exclude MDR within 1–2 days and should guide the choice of treatment regimen. 14. If DST is unavailable, first-line drug regimens should be used based on country-specific data on MDR prevalence, with adjustments made once DST results become available. 15. For new TB patients, if a sputum smear obtained at the end of the second month of intensive-phase treatment is positive, another smear should be obtained at the end of the third month. 16. If the third-month smear is positive, sputum culture and DST should be performed. 17. Sputum smear microscopy may be performed at the end of the intensive phase for smear-positive pulmonary TB patients treated with first-line drugs. 18. Sputum specimens should be collected after the first dose of intensive-phase treatment and at the end of the intensive phase (second month for new patients, third month for previously treated patients). 19. The proportion of smear-positive patients converting to negative at the end of the intensive phase is an indicator of TB program performance. 20. Treatment failure is defined as smear or culture positivity at the fifth month or later, or detection of MDR-TB at any point during therapy. 21. Causes of treatment failure may include poor supervision, poor patient adherence, substandard drug quality, inappropriate dosing, extensive cavitation, high initial bacterial load, co-morbid conditions, or MDR-TB. 22. Anti-TB drugs are grouped based on efficacy, experience of use, and drug class. First-line drugs are in Group 1, except streptomycin, which is classified with injectable agents in Group 2. 23. Second-line drugs (Groups 2–5) are used for MDR-TB treatment. Cross-resistance within drug families can occur due to resistance mutations in Mycobacterium tuberculosis. 24. MDR-TB treatment should include a fluoroquinolone, ethionamide (or prothionamide), and at least four second-line drugs likely to be effective, along with pyrazinamide during the intensive phase. 25. Ethambutol and Group 5 drugs may be used but are not part of the standard MDR-TB regimen. 26. Isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy is more common in pregnant women and individuals with HIV, alcohol dependency, malnutrition, diabetes, chronic liver disease, or renal failure. Preventive treatment with pyridoxine (10–25 mg/day) is recommended. 27. Management of anti-TB drug-induced hepatitis depends on the phase of therapy, severity of liver disease, severity of TB, and the ability to manage side effects. 28. If TB treatment is stopped due to hepatitis, wait for liver function tests to normalize and clinical symptoms to resolve before reintroducing anti-TB drugs. 29. In severe liver disease, a non-hepatotoxic regimen (streptomycin, ethambutol, and a fluoroquinolone) should be used for 18–24 months. 30. Reintroduce anti-TB drugs one at a time after hepatitis resolves, monitoring for recurrence of symptoms or abnormal liver function tests. 31. If rifampicin is implicated in hepatitis, a regimen without rifampicin (e.g., isoniazid, ethambutol, and streptomycin) can be used. 32. If isoniazid cannot be used, a regimen of rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for 6–9 months may be considered. 33. If neither isoniazid nor rifampicin can be used, a non-hepatotoxic regimen (streptomycin, ethambutol, and a fluoroquinolone) should be continued for 18–24 months. 34. For HIV-infected patients, intensified TB case finding and screening for latent TB infection are recommended. 35. Tuberculin skin testing (TST) is not required to initiate isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) in people living with HIV. 36. Interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) are not recommended for screening HIV-infected individuals for IPT eligibility due to limitations in distinguishing active TB from latent infection. 37. Adults and adolescents living with HIV should receive at least six months of IPT as part of comprehensive HIV care. 38. Providing IPT to people living with HIV does not increase the risk of developing isoniazid-resistant TB. 39. Children living with HIV who exhibit symptoms such as poor weight gain, fever, cough, or contact with a TB case should be evaluated for TB and other conditions. 40. HIV is the strongest risk factor for developing TB, with a 20–37 times higher risk in HIV-infected individuals compared to those without HIV. 41. TB accounts for over 25% of deaths in HIV-infected individuals. 42. WHO recommends 12 collaborative TB/HIV activities as part of core prevention, care, and treatment services for both diseases.
